extracted.intended_audience: readers/students of moral philosophy and ethics (general educated audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Schopenhauerian criteria for judging moral character and actions based on the concept of the will, the principium individuationis, and the relation between knowledge and disposition. Focuses on distinctions between bad, just, good, virtue, conscience, and love as sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good as relative (των προς τι)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every good is essentially relative; its being consists in its relation to a desiring will. 'Absolute good' is a contradiction in terms; 'highest good' (summum bonum) only metaphorically refers to the complete self-effacement and denial of the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding or judging 'good' requires locating how an object, action, or person relates to some desiring will. Do not treat 'good' as an absolute or permanent fulfilment; the only genuine end would be the (figurative) absence of will. Use this to avoid attributing absolute moral status to transient satisfactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad/wicked as denial of others' will
rubrics_metrics.description: A man is called 'bad' if he is disposed to do wrong whenever opportunity presents and, in asserting his will, denies the will which appears in other individuals—desiring their powers for his own ends or seeking to destroy them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate actions/characters by whether they assert their own will to the point of negating others' existence or interests. Root cause traced to high degree of egoism and excessive vehemence of the will; look for behavior that treats others as 'mere masks' or obstacles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cruelty as disinterested delight in others' suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: Wickedness proper, rising to cruelty, is the delight in the suffering of others which does not spring from mere egoism but is disinterested and an end in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish cruelty from instrumental harm: cruelty is not a means to the agent's satisfaction but a final end. Examples given: historical tyrants (Nero, Domitian) and instances where suffering is sought for its own sake. Treat delight in inflicted suffering as the mark of pure wickedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remorse (sting of conscience) as knowledge of unity and intensity of will
rubrics_metrics.description: Remorse springs from (1) a dim presentiment that the apparent separation of individuals is illusory (the one will appears in all) and (2) the self-knowledge of the vehemence with which the will asserts itself in the wicked individual; together these give the 'sting of conscience.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In judging moral culpability, consider whether the agent experiences this inward horror—recognition that his actions ultimately affect the one will and that his intense assertion of will binds him to the suffering he causes. Use remorse as evidence of latent recognition of moral truth and as distinct from mere social/legal sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as negation of the bad (voluntary recognition of moral limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntary justice is the disposition to recognise and observe the moral limits between wrong and right, even without external power—i.e., not carrying assertion of one's will so far as to deny others' wills. The just abstains from inflicting suffering, respects rights/property, and seeks not to compel others to serve his will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess justice by voluntary restraint rather than legal compulsion. Examples: willingness to support oneself, scepticism about inherited wealth, voluntary poverty as an extreme form. Distinguish political/legal rightness from moral justice (which concerns disposition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Goodness/disinterested virtue arises from direct intuitive knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine goodness and disinterested virtue do not proceed from abstract, communicable knowledge or moral theory but from an immediate, non-abstract intuitive knowledge that recognises in the individuality of others the same nature as in our own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating moral character, prioritize evidence of intuitive sympathy and conduct flowing from inner recognition rather than conformity to preached dogmas. Note that virtue cannot be taught simply by abstract doctrine—look for internally motivated deeds rather than externally induced actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motives (dogmas, custom, example) alter action not disposition (Velle non discitur)
rubrics_metrics.description: All abstract knowledge gives only motives, and motives only alter the expression of the will, not the will itself; moral theories, dogmas, customs, or example can shape outward conduct but not the inner disposition (the will).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between outward ethical behaviour (opera operata) and inner moral worth. In assessment, view actions motivated chiefly by reward/punishment or doctrinal belief with skepticism regarding their moral value. Use the maxim 'velle non discitur' to flag cases where behaviour is produced by external motives, not genuine change of will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degrees of penetration of the principium individuationis map to moral grades
rubrics_metrics.description: Penetration of the principium individuationis (seeing through the illusion of separateness) in varying degrees produces different moral qualities: a modest penetration yields justice (negation of bad); a higher penetration yields benevolence and love (good proper); a still higher degree leads to renunciation/asceticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging moral persons, consider how much they 'see through' individuation: do they merely refrain from harming (justice), actively mitigate suffering (benevolence), or renounce personal goods/pleasures (asceticism)? Use this as a spectrum for moral evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good conscience vs sting of conscience
rubrics_metrics.description: Good conscience is the satisfaction following a disinterested deed; it verifies the intuitive knowledge of unity with other beings and enlarges the heart. The sting of conscience is the inward pain accompanying bad disposition and wrongdoing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use presence of sustained good conscience (serenity, evenness of disposition) as an indicator of genuine virtue. Conversely, persistent inner torment or remorse signals recognition of wrongdoing and the depth of one's vehemence of will; distinguish internal moral feelings from external approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Altruistic sacrifice as consummation of perfect love
rubrics_metrics.description: When perfect goodness/love attains its highest form it will place other individuals completely on a level with itself and may sacrifice its own well-being or life for the well-being of many (examples: Codrus, Leonidas, Regulus, Socrates, Giordano Bruno).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate highest moral acts by willingness to sacrifice personal interests—even life—for the welfare of many or for universal truths. Use historical exemplars as paradigms but assess motive: true sacrifice springs from recognition of shared will, not desire for reward or reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love (αγαπη, caritas) is sympathy (knowledge of others' suffering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure love is essentially sympathy: the alleviation of suffering in others, since all wish-satisfaction merely removes pain; what motivates works of love is the knowledge of the suffering of others placed on a level with one's own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess loving actions by whether they attend to and seek to alleviate suffering, and by whether the agent truly identifies others' pain with their own. Recognize that love's practical expression will always be remedial (alleviating suffering) rather than producing positive permanent happiness.
